summary: Defines GMPLS routing and signaling extensions for networks in which routers take part in several different data plane switching layers or regions under one control plane. This is the multi-layer and multi-region network (MLN/MRN) case. It builds on the existing GMPLS framework.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6001 adds what GMPLS was missing for networks that mix several kinds of switching in one control plane. It defines a new piece of routing information that says how a node can move traffic between its own layers, a new way to exclude a switching capability from a path, and a new flag that sets up a link in the control plane before the resources behind it are committed.

questions: what is a hybrid node in gmpls
what is a virtual te link
what is a soft forwarding adjacency
subtitle: The GMPLS extensions that let one control plane steer paths across several layers and several technologies at once.

tldr.problem: A carrier's network mixes packet, layer 2, time-division, wavelength and fibre switching, and its control plane may span several regions. GMPLS was built to control that, but four things were missing: how a node says it can move traffic between its own layers, how a path says which switching capability to avoid, how a link is set up before it carries anything, and how it is removed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a routing extension, the Interface Adjustment Capability Descriptor, carried as a sub-TLV in OSPF and IS-IS, and two signalling extensions: a Switching Capability subobject in the exclude route object, and a CALL_ATTRIBUTES object with a Call Inheritance Flag. It also defines a pre-planned LSP flag, which sets up a forwarding adjacency in the control plane without yet taking resources in the data plane.
tldr.outcome: The result is that a single control plane can compute and signal paths through a multi-layer, multi-region network, while still being able to say which switching capabilities to avoid and to advertise a link before the resources behind it exist. The RFC keeps the new material inside one traffic engineering domain, under one administrator.

today: RFC 6001 is a Proposed Standard from October 2010 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It adds the routing and signalling extensions needed for multi-layer and multi-region networks to GMPLS, and it updates several documents in that family, including RFC 4202, RFC 4203, RFC 4206, RFC 5307, RFC 4874 and RFC 5420.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching extends MPLS to handle multiple switching technologies: packet switching, layer 2 switching, time-division multiplexing switching, wavelength switching and fibre switching. A GMPLS switching type describes the ability of a node to forward data of a particular data plane technology, and uniquely identifies a control plane LSP region.

A network comprising multiple switching types, for example packet switching and time-division multiplexing, controlled by a single GMPLS control plane instance is called a Multi-Region Network. A data plane layer is a collection of network resources capable of terminating and or switching data traffic of a particular format, and a network comprising transport nodes participating in different data plane switching layers controlled by a single GMPLS control plane instance is called a Multi-Layer Network.

The applicability of GMPLS to multiple switching technologies provides unified control and operations for both LSP provisioning and recovery. This document covers the elements of a single GMPLS control plane instance controlling multiple layers within a given traffic engineering domain, which is a group of label switching routers that enforces a common traffic engineering policy. A control plane instance can serve one, two or more layers. Other approaches, such as having multiple control plane instances serving disjoint sets of layers, are outside the scope of this document.

The requirements for multi-layer and multi-region networks are set out in RFC 5212, and are evaluated against the GMPLS protocols in RFC 5339, which identifies the areas where GMPLS protocol extensions are required. This document defines GMPLS routing and signalling extensions to cover those requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS already lets one control system drive a network that mixes packets, wavelengths and time slots. This RFC fills the gaps that a mixed network runs into: telling other routers what a node can do between its own layers, and saying which kind of switching a path should avoid.

sections.title: The Four Areas That Needed Extensions
sections.content:
Most multi-layer and multi-region requirements rely on mechanisms and procedures, such as local procedures and policies or specific traffic engineering mechanisms and algorithms, that are outside the scope of the GMPLS protocols and therefore need no protocol extensions.

Four areas did need extensions, as identified in RFC 5339.

The first is a routing extension for the advertisement of the internal adjustment capability of hybrid nodes, that is, nodes with more than one switching capability. The second is a signalling extension for constrained multi-region signalling, expressed as switching capability inclusion and exclusion, together with a Switching Capability subobject of the exclude route object, which was absent from the earlier definition of that object. The third is a signalling extension for the setup and deletion of virtual traffic engineering links, and for the exact trigger of their actual provisioning. The fourth is a routing and signalling extension for the graceful deletion of traffic engineering links.

The first three requirements are addressed in the following three sections of this document. The fourth is addressed in RFC 5710, with additional context provided by RFC 5817.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things were missing, and this RFC covers three of them. The fourth, removing a link without disturbing traffic, is covered elsewhere.

sections.title: The Interface Adjustment Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
In a multi-region network, a node with at least one interface that supports more than one switching capability is called a hybrid node. Its logical composition contains at least two distinct switching elements, interconnected by internal links that provide adjustment between the supported switching capabilities. Those internal links have finite capacities that must be taken into account when computing the path of a multi-region traffic engineering LSP, so advertising the internal adjustment capability is required, because it provides critical information when performing multi-region path computation.

These nodes, which host multiple interface switching capabilities, have to hold and advertise resource information on link states and topology like other nodes, and they may also have to consider the portions of internal node resources used to terminate hierarchical LSPs. In circuit switching technologies such as time-division multiplexing, wavelength switching and fibre switching, LSPs require resources allocated in a discrete manner. For example, a node with packet and wavelength hierarchical switching capability can switch a wavelength LSP, but cannot terminate it if there is no available adjustment capability between the wavelength and packet switching components.

The descriptor therefore discriminates the internal adjustment capability from the interface switching capability, which can already be inferred from the bandwidth available for each switching capability. It lets a node discriminate the remote nodes with respect to their adjustment capability, and so be selected during path computation.

The addition of the descriptor as a traffic engineering link attribute does not modify the format of the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor, and does not change how that sub-TLV is carried in the routing protocols or how it is processed when received. In OSPF the IACD sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV of the TE Link TLV, type 2, with type 25 and variable length. In IS-IS it is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended IS Reachability TLV with type 27, in an identical format, and the fields have the same processing and interpretation rules. Multiple IACD sub-TLVs may be present in a given link TLV.

The sub-TLV carries a lower switching capability and a lower encoding, an upper switching capability and an upper encoding, then a list of eight maximum LSP bandwidth values, one for each priority, in IEEE floating point format with priority 0 first, in units of bytes per second, and finally a variable field reserved for adjustment capability specific information. The lower switching capability must be set to the switching capability of the interface switching capability descriptor advertised for the link, or, if several are advertised, to the one the adjustment capacity is associated with. The upper encoding is set to the encoding of the available adjustment capacity, and to 0xFF when the corresponding upper switching capability has no access to the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: A node that speaks two kinds of switching at once has to say how much traffic it can shift from one to the other. The new routing sub-TLV carries that: which two layers it can move between, and how much bandwidth is left for it at each priority.

sections.title: Multi-Region Signalling and the Exclude Route Object
sections.content:
When a region boundary node receives a Path message, it determines whether it is at the edge of an LSP region with respect to the explicit route object carried in the message, then determines the other edge of the region using the interior gateway protocol database, and extracts from the explicit route object the sub-sequence of hops from itself to that other end. It then compares that sub-sequence with all the existing Forwarding Agency LSPs it has originated.

If a match is found, that Forwarding Agency LSP has enough unreserved bandwidth for the LSP being signalled, and the Generalized PID of the Forwarding Agency LSP is compatible with the Generalized PID of the LSP being signalled, the node uses it. The Path message for the original LSP is sent to the egress of the Forwarding Agency LSP, the previous hop is the address of the node at the head end of that LSP, and the explicit route object in the message is adjusted by removing the sub-sequence that lies in the Forwarding Agency LSP and replacing it with just the endpoint of that LSP. If no existing Forwarding Agency LSP is found, the node sets up a new one.

Applying that procedure in a multi-region environment may lead to single-hop Forwarding Agency LSPs between each pair of nodes, so it is consistent to provide enough signalling information to indicate which switching capability to use and over which link. In particular, when a traffic engineering link has multiple switching capabilities advertised in its interface switching capability descriptors, an explicit route object provides no mechanism to select a particular one.

To limit the modifications to existing RSVP-TE procedures, the RFC defines a new subobject of the exclude route object, the Switching Capability subobject, which enables the explicit identification of at least one switching capability to be excluded from the resource selection process. Including it as part of the exclude route object that indicates which capabilities have to be excluded over a specified link solves the ambiguous choice among the capabilities that might be used along a path, and gives the possibility of optimising resource use on a multi-region basis. Implicit inclusion is easily supported by explicitly excluding the others: to include wavelength switching, packet, layer 2, time-division and fibre switching all have to be excluded. The approach is to concentrate exclusions in the exclude route object and inclusions in the explicit route object, since the latter specifies the topological characteristics of the path to be signalled.

The Switching Capability subobject has type 35 and a length of 4. Its first bit says whether the capability must be excluded or should be avoided, its attribute field says that the capability should be excluded or avoided with respect to the preceding numbered or unnumbered interface subobject, and its last byte gives the switching capability value to be excluded. The subobject must follow the set of one or more numbered or unnumbered interface subobjects it refers to, and in the case of a loose-hop explicit route subobject it must precede the loose-hop subobject identifying the tail-end node or interface of the traversed regions. The RFC also complements the subobjects of the exclude route object with a Label subobject of type 3, whose encoding is that of the label subobject of the explicit route object apart from the L bit, and whose label values must be compatible with the switching capability being excluded.
sections.plainLanguage: When a path crosses the edge of a region, the node either reuses a tunnel it already has or sets one up. The new part lets the path say which kind of switching it does not want to use on a link, so the node does not have to guess between several options.

sections.title: Virtual Traffic Engineering Links
sections.content:
A virtual traffic engineering link is a link between two upper-layer nodes that is not associated with a fully provisioned Forwarding Agency LSP in a lower layer. It is advertised as any other link, and it represents the potential to set up such an LSP to support the link that has been advertised. Its flooding scope is within an interior gateway protocol area, as for any link.

Two techniques can be used for the setup, operation and maintenance of virtual links, and the RFC describes the protocol extensions for both.

The first is the edge-to-edge association, which does not require state maintenance on transit nodes and relies on extensions to the GMPLS RSVP-TE call procedure. It exchanges identification and traffic engineering attribute information directly between the endpoints of the link, which correspond to the head-end and tail-end points of the LSPs that will be established, and which must belong to the same LSP region. Once the call is established, the resulting association populates the local traffic engineering database, and the virtual link is advertised like any other, so it can attract traffic. When an upper-layer LSP tries to use it, one or more Forwarding Agency LSPs must be established to make the virtual link real and carry the traffic by nesting the upper-layer LSP inside them.

For that, a CALL_ATTRIBUTES object is introduced, modelled on the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object, used to signal the attributes required in support of a call or to indicate the nature or use of a call, and optionally used to report call operational state on a Notify message. Its object class is 202 of the form 11bbbbbb, which ensures that routers that do not recognise it pass it on transparently, and one class type is defined, 1 for Call Attributes. Its contents are encoded in Call Attributes TLVs, one or more of which may be present, with no ordering rules. The first of these, type 1, is the Call Attributes Flags TLV, an array of 32-bit units of flags numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero, whose length must always be a multiple of 4 bytes; unassigned bits are reserved and must be set to zero on transmission, and bits not present are treated as if they were present and zero. The first of those flags, bit 0, is the Call Inheritance Flag, which indicates that the association between the endpoints results in a virtual link advertisement. It must be set to 1 to have the association translated into a link advertisement, and by default it is set to 1. Setting it to 0 results in a hidden link, or in deleting the link advertisement if the association had already been established, in which case the corresponding Forwarding Agency LSP should also be torn down to prevent unused resources. The Notify message that establishes the association must carry an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object, so that unnumbered and numbered Forwarding Agency LSPs can be identified.

The second technique is the Soft Forwarding Adjacency, which sets up the Forwarding Agency LSP at the control plane level without actually committing resources in the data plane, so the LSP exists only in the control plane. Once it is established, the corresponding link can be advertised. Two techniques set up a Soft Forwarding Adjacency: setting up the LSP by precluding resource commitment during its establishment, which gives what are known as pre-planned LSPs, and making use of path-provisioned LSPs only, where there is no associated resource demand during establishment, which can be considered the RSVP-TE equivalent of the Null service type.

For the first, the RFC defines a Pre-Planned LSP flag in the existing Attributes Flags TLV, at bit 6. When it is 0 the LSP must be fully provisioned, and its absence is compliant with the ordinary signalling processing. When it is 1 the LSP must be provisioned in the control plane only, and no resources are committed at the data plane level. Committing data plane resources is done by re-signalling the same LSP with the flag set to 0, and it is recommended that no other modification is made to the other RSVP objects during that operation, so that each intermediate node is concerned only with the commitment of resources.

For the second, a path-provisioned LSP is an LSP established with zero bandwidth, which differs from a pre-planned LSP, which is established with a bandwidth value that is not committed. For packet switching the peak data rate of the IntServ objects must be set to 0, and for layer 2 switching the committed and excess information rates and burst sizes must be set to 0. Provisioning a time-division or wavelength LSP with zero bandwidth is not currently possible, because the exchanged label value is tightly coupled with resource allocation, so a null label value is used to prevent resource allocation in the data plane; on commitment, the actual label value is exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can be advertised before anything is built to carry it. Two ways are given: the two ends talk directly to each other and agree on it, or a tunnel is set up in the control plane with no resources reserved yet. When traffic needs the link, the resources are committed.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The new objects and procedures run within a given traffic engineering domain, a group of label switching routers that enforces a common traffic engineering policy, so the extensions are expected to run in the context of a consistent policy. Specifying such a policy is outside the scope of the document.

Within such a domain, edge routers are distinguished from intermediate routers. Edge routers must be able to process Call Attributes if the edge-to-edge association method is selected. In that domain, intermediate routers are by definition transparent to the call processing. If the Soft Forwarding Adjacency method is used for creating virtual links, then edge and intermediate routers must support processing of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object as described in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: These extensions only work inside one traffic engineering domain, under one policy, and the routers in the middle of a domain do not have to understand them: they pass the new objects along unexamined.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations beyond those already detailed in RFC 5920, which describes the MPLS and GMPLS security threats, the related defensive techniques, and the mechanisms for detection and reporting. The applicability of the extensions is limited to a single traffic engineering domain, which is under the authority of a single administrative entity, and the multiple switching layers within that domain are under the control of a single GMPLS control plane instance.

Call initiation must nevertheless remain strictly under the control of the traffic engineering domain administrator. To prevent any abuse of call setup, edge nodes must ensure the isolation of their call controller, that is, it must not be reachable through external traffic engineering domains. To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks, security associations must be established between the edge nodes that initiate and terminate calls, and the Internet Key Exchange protocol must be used for the mutual authentication and the establishment and maintenance of those associations.
sections.plainLanguage: The new features stay inside one administrative domain, so the usual GMPLS security analysis still applies. But setting up a call between two edge routers is a privileged action, so the call controller must not be reachable from outside the domain, and the two ends must authenticate each other with IKE.

items.title: Adjustment capability
items.text: A routing extension so that hybrid nodes can advertise the internal adjustment capability between their switching components. Addressed in this RFC.

items.title: Switching capability exclusion
items.text: A signalling extension for constrained multi-region signalling, using a Switching Capability subobject of the exclude route object. Addressed in this RFC.

items.title: Virtual TE links
items.text: A signalling extension for the setup and deletion of virtual traffic engineering links, and for the trigger of their actual provisioning. Addressed in this RFC.

items.title: Graceful TE link deletion
items.text: Routing and signalling extensions for graceful traffic engineering link deletion. Addressed in RFC 5710, with additional context in RFC 5817.

fields.name: Lower Switching Capability
fields.desc: The lower switching capability associated with the Lower Encoding field, set to the switching capability of the ISCD advertised for this link.

fields.name: Lower Encoding
fields.desc: One of the LSP Encoding Type values.

fields.name: Upper Switching Capability
fields.desc: The upper switching capability, one of the values defined for the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor.

fields.name: Upper Encoding
fields.desc: The encoding of the available adjustment capacity, or 0xFF when that switching capability has no access to the wire.

viz.caption: THE XRO SWITCHING CAPABILITY SUBOBJECT (RFC 6001 SECTION 4.1.1)

fields.name: L
fields.desc: 0 means the attribute must be excluded, 1 means it should be avoided.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: The type of the subobject, 35 for Switching Capability.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The total length of the subobject in bytes, including the Type and Length fields. The length is 4.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.desc: 0 is reserved; 1 means the switching capability should be excluded or avoided with respect to the preceding interface subobject.

fields.name: Switching Cap
fields.desc: The switching capability value to be excluded.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO SET UP A VIRTUAL LINK

cells: A call between the two endpoints, exchanging identification and traffic engineering attributes directly
A forwarding adjacency LSP in the control plane, with no resources committed in the data plane
The LSP exists in the control plane domain
Advertised like any other link once the call is established
Advertised like any other link once the adjacency is established
One or more forwarding agency LSPs are established when traffic needs the link
Resources are committed later by re-signalling the same LSP with the Pre-Planned flag cleared
